title: Stagewise latency digest
content:
Quick notes / running log: stagewise latency digest

Context
- Goal: get a compact, actionable view of end-to-end token latency broken down by logical stages (tokenize, compile/load, kv lookup, batch wait, model compute, postprocess, egress) for the hosted inference fleet. Focus on p50/p95/p99 across a representative sample and identify small set of quick wins for p99 regressions.
- Motivation: recent customer report (CS ticket CS-918) of intermittent p99 spikes ~300ms above baseline for short completions (~10–20 tokens). SRE flagged elevated queue lengths in some pools during microburst windows.

Dataset & selection
- Period: 2024-10-10 -> 2024-10-17 (7d).
- Source: sampled traces from tracing service (trace sampling policy: 2% global + targeted sampling for requests > p95).
- Cohorts: short (<=32 tokens), mid (33–128), long (>128); coldstart vs warmed (kv cache miss ratio > 0.7 labelled cold). Model variants included: rwd-13B/float16 and rwd-13B/q4f16.
- Excluded warmup artifacts: traces that include autoscaling pod spinups or infra reboots (filtered via event tags).

Methodology
- Reconstruct E2E timeline by aligning spans, normalize to token emit boundary where possible. Stages defined as:
  1) tokenize: raw request -> first token-ready event
  2) compile/load: JIT/kernel selection + model load (if any)
  3) kv-lookup: prefix KV cache interactions + network/hotshard hits
  4) batch-wait: time waiting in batching queue before batch dispatched
  5) model-compute: attention + transformer compute until token produced (includes KV writeback)
  6) postprocess: detokenize, filters, function-calls glue
  7) egress: network send + client ack time
- For each trace compute per-stage durations and global p50/p95/p99. Use median-of-means to reduce extreme sample influence.
- Instrumentation caveat: some older traces lack fine-grained KV span (pre-2024-06 agents) — those were dropped from kv metrics but kept for E2E baseline.

Summary numbers (cohort: short completions, warmed)
- Global E2E: p50=37ms, p95=86ms, p99=185ms
- Per-stage p50/p95/p99 (ms):
  tokenize: 1 / 2 / 5
  compile/load: 2 / 4 / 12
  kv-lookup: 3 / 12 / 42
  batch-wait: 8 / 32 / 110
  model-compute: 15 / 28 / 60
  postprocess: 4 / 6 / 10
  egress: 4 / 6 / 20

Observation highlights
- batch-wait dominates p99 for short warmed requests (110ms contribution at p99). This tracks to bursty arrival patterns where batch windows grow to absorb a few high-latency requests.
- kv-lookup p99 tail is non-trivial (42ms): correlated with cross-shard misses and occasional RPC retries (see trace examples in linked PR).
- model-compute p95 is reasonable but p99 shows heavy variance — likely due to ephemeral contention on GPU SMs when background kernels run (profiling flag show kernel preemption events).
- compile/load is small overall, but when it spikes (p99=12ms) it's correlated with rare runtime re-jit activity for quant kernels (observed ~0.6% of traces).

Hypotheses (ranked)
1) Batch window policy (fixed 5ms target) scales poorly under certain microburst patterns — increasing dynamic early-release could reduce p99 by ~30–50ms.
2) KV cache routing misrouting increases RPCs for a tail subset; sample indicates a small hot-shard imbalance across two ASGs.
3) GPU-side interference from non-inference workloads (model compile/metrics flush) can spike model-compute for <1% of requests.

Trace exemplar (short warmed, p99)
- timeline (ms): tokenize(1) -> kv-lookup(38) -> batch-wait(110) -> model-compute(25) -> postprocess(4) -> egress(7) -> total ~185
- notes: kv-lookup here includes two RPC retries; batch window shows a 5x increase vs median due to synchronous flushing for prior large batch.

Quick wins and experiments to run (<=2 weeks)
- Experiment A: enable dynamic batch early-release (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/842) on 10% of traffic for short cohort. Measure p99 delta after 24h. Expected p99 reduction ~30ms, cost +/-1–2% CPU.
- Experiment B: add per-shard kv miss logging (low-overhead tracer) and run on affected ASGs to confirm hot-shard distribution. Target: reduce kv p99 by identifying two offending keys.
- Experiment C: schedule low-priority background kernels to fenced compute slot on busiest nodes and measure model-compute p99 effect.

Longer-term work (quarter roadmap items)
- Adaptive batching using arrival-time prediction (model arrival jitter to set per-batch timeouts). Prototype Q1.
- KV cache shard rebalancer + health-signal-based routing (follow-up to RUN-3124).
- Trace-sample enrichment to include GPU kernel telemetry for tighter attribution.

Action items (owner, ETA)
- Nina: roll out Experiment A to dev canary (10% small cohort) — ETA 2024-11-04.
- Samir: implement low-overhead kv miss tracer + dashboard — ETA 2024-11-11.
- Elena: run node-scheduling experiment for background kernel fencing on two worst ASGs — ETA 2024-11-08.
- Jose: collect full-day p99 snapshots post-experiment and run the median-of-means reanalysis — ETA 2024-11-13.

Open questions / unknowns
- Is batch-window growth here an emergent property of certain client usage patterns (client-side fanout) vs internal arrival bursts? Need to pull a sample of request arrival histograms.
- How much of kv-lookup tail is network vs server CPU? Need instrumented per-RPC timing.
- Are p99 model-compute spikes more frequent on a single GPU model type (A100 vs H100)? Need to join with infra inventory and isolate by GPU generation.

Notes to self
- Attach 3 representative traces to PR and to RUN-3124.
- Check whether the streaming path shows different batch-wait characteristics — streaming clients may bypass batching or use small windows.
- Re-run cohort with coldstart-only to contrast warm-vs-cold kv impact (I expect cold p99 to be >2x).

Appendix: quick sample commands
- query traces: 
  ./tools/tracequery --start 2024-10-10 --end 2024-10-17 --service serving --tag cohort:short --sample 0.02 > short-traces.json
- compute stage stats: 
  python infra/analysis/stage_stats.py --traces short-traces.json --out short-stage-stats.csv

If we get the experiment A results showing ~30ms improvement at p99, we should consider rolling dynamic early-release to 50% and assessing cost impact.

End of digest.
